title: Data science from the ground up
summary: Turn a messy question into a useful answer. Meet Python, notebooks, and your first DataFrame.
analogy: Think of data science as detective work: ask a question, gather clues, check them, find a pattern, and explain what to do next.
concepts: The six-step loop
Question → Data → Clean → Analyze → Model → Communicate. You can loop back when the evidence changes your question. A model is optional; a useful decision is the goal.
Your notebook is a workbench
Colab lets you mix Python cells, output, and explanations. Run the setup cell first. Names only exist after their defining cell has run; restart and run all to check reproducibility.
Python building blocks
Variables name values. Lists store ordered items; dictionaries map keys to values. Loops repeat work, if chooses a branch, and a function packages reusable logic with def and return.
A DataFrame is a programmable table
Rows are records; columns are fields. Read a CSV with pd.read_csv(), then inspect head(), shape, info(), and describe(). A column that looks numeric can still be stored as text.
Five facts before any model
Count rows and columns, check the date range, count distinct products, and total revenue. Clear labels let another person check your work.
task: Load a sales table and print five labeled facts: rows, columns, date range, unique products, and total revenue.
pitfall: The slides refer to supplied CSV files, but those files were not attached. The practice notebooks use clearly labeled synthetic data instead.

quiz.q: What should happen before modeling?
options: Ask a clear question and inspect the data
quiz.why: The question defines success, and inspection helps prevent confident answers built on bad data.

quiz.q: Which command shows column types and non-null counts?
quiz.why: info() reports column dtypes and non-null counts. shape gives dimensions; head() previews rows.

title: Data manipulation with pandas
summary: Select the right rows, group the evidence, and turn a table into a ranked answer.
analogy: Imagine sorting students into faculty teams, calculating each team's average, then putting the teams on a leaderboard. That is filter → group → aggregate → sort.
concepts: Series or DataFrame?
df['gpa'] is one Series. df[['gpa']] is a DataFrame with one column. The extra brackets change the type, which matters when a function expects a table.
Labels versus positions
Use .loc for labels and column names; label slices include the end label. Use .iloc for integer positions; the end position is excluded, just like ordinary Python slicing.
A mask is a yes/no checklist
df['gpa'] > 3 returns one boolean per row. Put the mask inside df[...] to keep True rows. Combine masks with & or | and parentheses around each condition.
Split, apply, combine
groupby splits rows into groups, applies a calculation such as mean or sum, then combines the results. Named .agg() gives readable output columns; pivot_table lays grouped results out as a grid.
Rank and derive

sort_values orders rows; nlargest gives a top-N list; groupby(...).rank() ranks within groups. Prefer whole-column arithmetic and np.where. Use apply(axis=1) when custom row logic is needed. map, replace, and cut recode values.
task: Filter to students who passed. Group by faculty, calculate student count, average GPA, and total study hours, then sort by GPA.
pitfall: Use & rather than Python's and for pandas masks. Protect division by zero when creating ratios. The copied rank example fixes a slide line-wrap that would otherwise be invalid Python.

quiz.q: What does df[['gpa']] return?
quiz.why: A list of column names inside the brackets preserves the two-dimensional DataFrame.

quiz.q: Which pattern gives an average GPA per faculty?
quiz.why: groupby separates faculties before calculating each group's mean.

title: Data cleaning & wrangling
summary: Find missing values, fix types, join tables, and make the whole cleanup repeatable.
analogy: Cleaning data is like checking ingredients before cooking. A missing ingredient, a duplicate order, or a mislabeled jar changes the result even if the recipe is perfect.
concepts: Audit before fixing
Count nulls, duplicates, invalid ranges, and inconsistent category labels. Missing values can be NaN, blank strings, or special codes; inspect what they mean before treating them alike.
Dropping and filling make assumptions

dropna removes observations; fillna replaces missing values. Median resists extreme values. Forward fill only makes sense when the ordering and meaning justify carrying a previous observation forward.
Keys and types matter
Choose the record's real key before dropping duplicates. Convert numeric strings and dates, strip spaces, and standardize case. Check dtypes and row counts again afterward.
Reshape without losing meaning

merge matches keys, concat stacks tables, melt makes wide data long, and pivot_table summarizes into a grid. An inner join keeps matches; a left join preserves left-side records but can multiply them if keys repeat.
One reusable cleaning function
Copy the input, apply documented steps in a deliberate order, and return the clean result. Keep raw data so fixes can be audited and rerun.
task: Write clean(raw) to handle duplicate student IDs, numeric GPA, missing age, and inconsistent faculty names. Compare before-and-after counts.
pitfall: A median is not automatically the right replacement. For predictive models, learn imputation values on the training data only. Use merge validation when you expect a many-to-one or one-to-one relationship.

quiz.q: Why check row counts after a merge?
quiz.why: Repeated join keys can create multiple matches and inflate totals.

quiz.q: Which fill is less sensitive to very large numeric outliers?
quiz.why: The median uses the middle position rather than the magnitude of every observation.

title: Exploratory data analysis
summary: Read distributions, discover relationships, and turn unusual values into better questions.
analogy: EDA is walking around a new neighborhood before drawing a map. You notice the busy streets, quiet corners, and surprising exceptions first.
concepts: Explore, then confirm
EDA generates hypotheses. Confirmatory analysis tests a specific hypothesis. Do not treat a pattern discovered in one dataset as proven just because it looks convincing.
Understand the shape

Histograms show how values are distributed across bins. Boxplots summarize median, quartiles, and flagged extremes. Skewness describes asymmetry; kurtosis describes tail behavior relative to a reference distribution.
Correlation is a clue
Pearson correlation measures linear association from -1 to +1. A value near zero can still hide a strong nonlinear relationship. Scatterplots help reveal what a single number misses.
Flag outliers; investigate first
IQR = Q3 − Q1. Common fences are Q1 − 1.5×IQR and Q3 + 1.5×IQR. A z-score measures distance in standard deviations; the usual |z| > 3 rule needs distributional judgment.
Write testable questions
Replace 'these groups look different' with a specific comparison, defined outcome, and proposed check. Separate observation from interpretation and consider confounders.
task: Plot distributions, inspect a correlation matrix, flag outliers, and write three hypotheses with a proposed way to test each.
pitfall: Correlation does not establish causation. An extreme value may be a valuable real observation rather than an error to delete.

quiz.q: You flag a very high purchase value. What next?
options: Investigate whether it is an error or a real event
quiz.why: A large real purchase may be an important business signal.

quiz.q: Pearson correlation near zero means…
quiz.why: Nonlinear relationships can exist even when Pearson correlation is near zero.

title: Visualization & storytelling
summary: Choose charts with purpose and connect them into a story people can act on.
analogy: A chart is a sentence. Three well-chosen charts can form a short argument: here is the situation, here is the problem, and here is our next move.
concepts: Match the chart to the question
Use bars for category comparisons, lines for time trends, histograms or boxplots for distributions, and scatterplots for relationships. Choose the question before the chart.
Figure is the canvas; Axes is a plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots() creates a canvas and a plotting area. Use ax methods to draw, label, and annotate. Multiple Axes let you compare related views side by side.
Seaborn supplies statistical grammar
Pass a DataFrame and column names. hue separates categories, heatmap reveals a matrix, and distribution plots show shape. Know what aggregation and uncertainty a plotting function computes.
Situation → complication → resolution
Set the baseline, identify the change or problem, then recommend a response. Each chart should earn its place by supporting one step in that argument.
Title with the finding
A useful title tells the reader what changed. Include units, readable labels, and a focused annotation. Avoid decoration that competes with the evidence.
task: Build three annotated charts that tell one coherent story, then write the recommendation in a single sentence.
pitfall: A plotted uncertainty band is not automatically a prediction interval. Read the chart function's statistical behavior and describe what the band represents.

quiz.q: Which chart best shows monthly revenue over two years?
quiz.why: A line preserves the ordered progression of time.

quiz.q: Which title communicates a finding?
quiz.why: A finding-led title tells the reader what to notice, provided the data supports it.

title: Sales performance analysis
summary: Audit retail data, calculate KPIs, and find the segments behind the headline.
analogy: A shop's total revenue is the scoreboard. Growth, margin, time trends, and category breakdowns explain how that score happened.
concepts: Start with the retail brief
Ask where the business is growing, where it is losing ground, and what leadership should do. Define the time range and unit of analysis before calculating.
Audit transactions
Check dates, missing values, duplicate IDs, price, and quantity. Derive revenue = price × quantity only after understanding returns and invalid values. Add year, month, and quarter as needed.
Calculate meaningful KPIs
Revenue is a sum; growth compares the current period with a previous period; margin is profit divided by revenue. State the denominator and units so a percentage is interpretable.
Respect time
Aggregate by year-month rather than month number alone when data spans years. Rolling means smooth noise but can hide sudden changes. Compare similar seasonal periods when interpreting growth.
Segment the headline
Group by category and region. An overall average can hide a growing segment and a declining one. Rank products, then ask how size, growth, and profitability differ.
task: Add one original KPI to the retail analysis, compute it with a clear definition, and write the decision it supports.
pitfall: Average line-item margins are not the same as total profit / total revenue. Growth from a zero baseline is undefined; handle it explicitly.

quiz.q: Revenue is 200 and cost is 150. What is margin?
quiz.why: Profit is 50. Margin = 50 / 200 = 25%.

quiz.q: Why avoid grouping only by month number over multiple years?
options: It mixes January from different years
quiz.why: Use year-month periods to keep separate years distinct.

title: Insights reports & dashboards
summary: Build interactive charts, curate a dashboard, and write a memo with a clear recommendation.
analogy: Your notebook is the kitchen; the dashboard is the meal. The reader needs the carefully chosen result, not every experiment you tried.
concepts: Curate the message
Choose a few findings that answer the brief. Each needs evidence and an implication. A correct chart without a useful question still creates work for the reader.
Plotly adds exploration
px.bar, px.line, and px.scatter create interactive views with hover details and zoom. Keep the same chart-selection discipline you use for static plots.
Show hierarchy and trade-offs
Sunburst shows nested categories; bubble scatter can combine margin, revenue, volume, and category. Use these only when the extra dimensions help answer the question.
Assemble a coherent panel
Put headline KPIs first, trends second, and detailed breakdowns afterward. Keep filters and units consistent. Export interactive Plotly figures to HTML for sharing.
Write the three-point memo
For each of three findings, give a specific statement, supporting evidence, and business implication. End with one recommendation and identify uncertainty or what to monitor.
task: Write a one-page memo with three evidenced findings and one recommendation. Ask a peer whether they know what action to take.
pitfall: Interactivity cannot rescue an unclear question. Avoid implying that an observational chart proves why something changed.

quiz.q: What belongs in an insight memo?
options: A finding, evidence, implication, and recommendation
quiz.why: A decision-maker needs the meaning of the analysis and a next action.

quiz.q: What does a sunburst show well?
quiz.why: Nested rings represent parent-child categories and their contributions.

title: RFM customer segmentation
summary: Describe customer behavior with three numbers, then design a different action for each group.
analogy: A café owner remembers who visited recently, who comes often, and who spends the most. RFM turns that memory into a repeatable table.
concepts: Change the unit of analysis
Move from transactions or products to one row per customer. Choose a snapshot date and observation window so comparisons have a consistent meaning.
R, F, and M
Recency = days since last purchase, lower is more recent. Frequency = number of purchases. Monetary = total spend. If each order has multiple lines, count distinct order IDs.
Score in the right direction
qcut makes rank-based tiers. Reverse recency labels so low days get a high score. Frequency and monetary usually score high-is-high. Ties can prevent distinct quantile boundaries.
Name useful segments
Combine scores into business rules for Champions, loyal customers, at-risk customers, and others. State rule precedence, because overlapping conditions can assign different labels.
Profile, then act
Compare segment size, value, and behavior. Champions might receive VIP access; at-risk customers might receive a win-back test. Monitor outcomes instead of assuming the label guarantees a response.
task: Build one RFM row per customer, assign transparent segment rules, profile the groups, and propose one action for each.
pitfall: The slide uses count(order_id), which counts rows. Use nunique if transactions contain multiple lines per order. Arbitrary tie-breaking for qcut can split identical customers; document the choice.

quiz.q: A customer purchased yesterday. Their recency is…
quiz.why: Recency counts elapsed days, so a recent purchase means a smaller value.

quiz.q: An order has three product rows. How should purchase frequency count it?
quiz.why: Count unique order IDs when the intended frequency is number of purchases.

title: Clustering with K-Means
short: Let the data draw the groups
summary: Scale features, find clusters, choose K, and give each group a business meaning.
analogy: Imagine placing meeting points on a map. Each person joins the nearest meeting point; then each point moves to the center of its group. Repeat until the groups settle.
concepts: Unsupervised means no target labels
Clustering groups observations by similarity without a known correct class. Results depend on the features, preprocessing, distance measure, and chosen algorithm.
Scale before measuring distance
StandardScaler subtracts each feature's training mean and divides by its standard deviation. This prevents monetary units from overwhelming features measured on much smaller scales.
Assign, move, repeat
K-Means assigns points to the closest center and moves each center to its assigned points' mean. A seed helps reproducibility; use an explicit n_init=10 for multiple initializations.
Choose K with evidence and purpose

Inertia decreases as K increases. Look for diminishing returns, inspect silhouette scores, and ask whether the groups are useful and stable. Silhouette needs at least two nonempty clusters and fewer clusters than samples.
Interpret and compare
Profile clusters in original units. Cluster 0 is only an ID, not a ranking. Compare with RFM rules using a crosstab. GMM provides soft membership probabilities instead of only hard assignments.
task: Scale RFM features, compare candidate K values, fit a final clustering, profile it, and compare it with rule-based segments.
pitfall: n_init='auto' does not always run several starts; behavior depends on initialization and version. Rules and clusters need not agree. Standardizing does not guarantee meaningful clusters.

quiz.q: Why scale RFM before K-Means?
options: To avoid large-unit features dominating distance
quiz.why: Distance is affected by each feature's numeric scale.

quiz.q: Is cluster 0 necessarily better than cluster 1?
quiz.why: You need cluster profiles to understand their meaning.

title: ML foundations & pipelines
summary: Learn the shared workflow behind estimators and evaluate them on genuinely unseen data.
analogy: Training is studying with practice questions. Testing is the exam. Looking at the exam answers while preparing makes your score look good but tells you little about learning.
concepts: Choose the right task
Supervised learning uses known target labels. Regression predicts a number; classification predicts a category. Unsupervised learning looks for structure without target labels.
X is input; y is the target
Choose features available at prediction time. Split data, fit on training data, predict on held-out data, and evaluate with a metric that matches the decision.
One estimator interface
fit learns parameters, predict applies them, and score gives an estimator's default metric. Regression score is often R²; classification score is often accuracy. Explicit metrics are clearer.
Keep the final test set untouched

Cross-validation rotates validation folds within training data. Use it to compare settings, then evaluate once on the held-out test set. Time-ordered and grouped data need appropriate splitting strategies.
Bundle preprocessing with the model
Pipeline fits imputation and scaling inside each training fold when cross-validated as a whole. That prevents preprocessing leakage, but not target leakage or bad split design.
task: Build an imputer → scaler → estimator pipeline. Split before fitting, cross-validate on training data, and evaluate on the held-out test set.
pitfall: A Pipeline does not make every kind of leakage impossible. Features derived from future information, duplicated entities across splits, or test-driven model tuning can still leak information.

quiz.q: Where should a scaler learn its mean for supervised evaluation?
options: The training data within each fold
quiz.why: Learning from test values exposes information that should be held out.

quiz.q: What should cross-validation compare before final testing?
options: Candidate models or settings using training data
The test set repeatedly until the score is good
quiz.why: Keep the final test independent of model-selection decisions.

title: Regression, Ridge & Lasso
summary: Fit a baseline, inspect its errors, and test whether regularization improves generalization.
analogy: A flexible ruler can bend through every practice point. Regularization asks it to stay simpler so it has a better chance of fitting tomorrow's points too.
concepts: OLS minimizes squared residuals
Linear regression predicts a number from a weighted sum of features plus an intercept. Coefficients describe conditional associations, holding other included features fixed.
Read the error, not just the line
RMSE expresses typical error on the target's scale while penalizing large errors. R² compares squared errors with a mean baseline; it can be negative on held-out data.
Inspect residuals and collinearity
Residuals are actual minus predicted. Patterns can suggest missing structure or changing variance. Highly correlated predictors can make individual coefficients unstable.
Bias and variance trade off
Too much flexibility can memorize noise. Too little can miss real structure. Compare training and validation behavior instead of assuming a more complex model is better.
Ridge shrinks; Lasso can select
Ridge uses an L2 penalty; Lasso uses L1 and can set coefficients exactly to zero. Scale features and select alpha through cross-validation of the full pipeline.
task: Compare OLS and Ridge using the same folds and error metric. Report the measured difference; improvement is not guaranteed.
pitfall: A coefficient is not automatically a causal effect, and Lasso's selected features are not guaranteed to be the true drivers. Ridge does not guarantee every coefficient is nonzero.

quiz.q: Can held-out R² be negative?
options: No, it is always between 0 and 1
Yes, when squared error is worse than the mean baseline
quiz.why: Held-out predictions can perform worse than simply predicting the test target mean.

quiz.q: Which penalty can set coefficients exactly to zero?
options: Any model with a random seed
quiz.why: L1 regularization can produce sparse coefficient vectors.

title: Classification & ensembles
summary: Predict churn, tune the decision threshold, compare ensembles, and explain a prediction.
analogy: A smoke alarm has two costs: missing a fire and sounding when nothing is wrong. Classification thresholds balance those errors for the decision you actually face.
concepts: Probability is not a decision
Logistic regression returns class probabilities. A threshold converts them to labels. Lowering the positive threshold generally catches more positives and also creates more false positives.
Bagging versus boosting
Random Forest combines trees trained with randomness. Gradient boosting builds a sequence that improves a loss function. Neither is guaranteed to beat every simpler model; compare fairly.
Read the confusion matrix

True positives are correctly flagged churners; false positives are false alarms; false negatives are missed churners; true negatives are correct non-churn predictions. Precision asks how trustworthy alerts are; recall asks how many churners are caught.
Match metrics to the problem

F1 balances precision and recall. ROC-AUC measures ranking over thresholds. For rare positive events, also inspect precision-recall behavior, calibration, and decision costs; accuracy alone can hide failure.
Explain the model, not causality

SHAP attributes a model's output to features relative to a background. Summary plots show patterns across cases; waterfall plots explain one output. The explained units depend on the model and explainer configuration.
task: Fit a logistic baseline and a Random Forest, evaluate them on the same held-out split, and explain one prediction. Keep threshold and model selection separate from the final test.
pitfall: The slide's waterfall snippet passes legacy SHAP arrays; modern waterfall plots need an Explanation for one sample and one output. The practice notebook demonstrates this explicitly.

quiz.q: If churn is rare, why can accuracy mislead?
options: Predicting no churn for everyone can score highly
quiz.why: The majority class can dominate accuracy even when the model catches no churners.

quiz.q: What does a SHAP explanation establish?
options: That changing a feature causes the outcome
How features contributed to a model output
quiz.why: SHAP explains model behavior; it does not establish causal effects or guarantee fairness.
